introduction-firecracker-the-microvm.core: Lambda runs each function in a Firecracker microVM: a minimal KVM-based virtual machine that boots in ~125 ms with ~5 MB overhead. That gives VM-level isolation between tenants with container-like density and speed, which is how AWS packs thousands of functions per host safely.

first_principles.problem: Containers share a kernel (weaker isolation); full VMs are too slow and heavy for per-request scaling.
derivation: **Strip** the VM to essentials (virtio net/block, no BIOS).

analogy.title: Pop-up shops in a shopping centre
analogy.story: Each gets its own locked unit, set up in minutes, many per floor.
analogy.breaks: Pop-up shops stay for weeks; microVMs live for minutes to hours.

check.q: Why does Lambda use microVMs instead of plain containers?
check.a: MicroVMs give hardware-level isolation between tenants while still booting quickly and densely.

the-lambda-lifecycle-cold-starts.core: A Lambda execution environment goes through Init (download code, start runtime, run initialisation code outside the handler), Invoke (run the handler, possibly many times while warm) and Shutdown. A cold start happens when no warm environment is available, so Init adds latency; warm invokes reuse connections and caches.

first_principles.problem: p99 latency spikes to 3 seconds on the first requests after quiet periods.
truths: Init cost depends on package size and runtime.
derivation: Put **reusable setup outside the handler** (clients, connections).

analogy.title: Opening a restaurant kitchen
analogy.story: The first order waits while ovens heat; later orders are fast while the kitchen stays open.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants close on schedule; Lambda recycles environments unpredictably.

code.text:
import boto3
ddb = boto3.resource('dynamodb').Table('orders')   # init once per environment

def handler(event, context):
    return ddb.get_item(Key={'id': event['id']})['Item']

check.q: Why place SDK clients outside the handler?
check.a: They're created once during Init and reused across warm invocations.

snapstart-cheating-the-cold-start.core: SnapStart (Java, Python, .NET) runs Init once when you publish a version, snapshots the initialised microVM's memory and disk, and restores from that snapshot on cold start, cutting startup from seconds to sub-second. Code must handle uniqueness and connections restored from a snapshot (runtime hooks).

first_principles.problem: A Spring Boot Lambda takes 6 seconds to cold start.
truths: Init work is mostly identical each time.
Restoring memory is faster than recomputing it.
Snapshots duplicate state such as random seeds.
derivation: **Re-seed** randomness and refresh connections after restore.

analogy.title: Resuming a saved game instead of replaying the intro
analogy.story: You load straight to where everything is set up.
analogy.breaks: Saved games are single-player; one snapshot seeds many environments, so unique values must be regenerated.

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: Regenerate UUID seeds in after-restore hook.

check.a: State captured in the snapshot (random seeds, connections, unique IDs) is duplicated across restored environments.

concurrency-reserved-vs-provisioned.core: Concurrency is the number of in-flight invocations (≈ requests/s × duration). Accounts have a regional limit (default 1,000). Reserved concurrency guarantees and caps a function's share; provisioned concurrency keeps N environments pre-initialised to eliminate cold starts, at extra cost.

first_principles.problem: One runaway function consumes all account concurrency and throttles critical ones, while the checkout API suffers cold starts.
derivation: **Reserve** for critical functions (and cap noisy ones).

analogy.title: Restaurant tables
analogy.story: Reserved tables guarantee (and limit) a party's seats; provisioned tables are already set with food on them.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants can turn people away politely; throttled events may be retried or lost depending on the source.

example.title: Capacity planning
flow: Image resizer: reserved max 100 to protect others

check.q: A function handles 50 req/s at 2 s each. What concurrency does it need?

lambda-layers-sharing-code-and-dependenc.core: Layers are versioned zip archives (libraries, runtimes, shared code, extensions) mounted under /opt in a function's environment. Up to five per function, sharing dependencies across many functions and keeping deployment packages small. The 250 MB unzipped total limit still applies; container images allow up to 10 GB.

first_principles.problem: Twenty functions each bundle the same 40 MB dependency, slowing deploys and drifting versions.
truths: Shared code should be versioned once.
Dependencies must match runtime and architecture.
derivation: **Package** shared libs into a layer (python/ or nodejs/ path).

analogy.title: A shared toolbox in a workshop
analogy.story: Everyone uses the same tools from one shelf instead of carrying their own.
analogy.breaks: Shared tools update for everyone; layers are pinned per function version, so upgrades are explicit.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Functions ship only their own code.

code.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt -t python/
zip -r deps.zip python
aws lambda publish-layer-version --layer-name deps --zip-file fileb://deps.zip \
  --compatible-runtimes python3.12 --compatible-architectures arm64

check.q: Where are layer contents available inside the function?

event-source-mappings-the-poller-fleet.core: For pull-based sources (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, Kafka, MQ), Lambda runs a managed poller fleet (event source mapping) that reads batches and invokes your function. You tune batch size, batching window, concurrency, parallelisation factor, filtering and failure handling (partial batch responses, bisect, DLQ/on-failure destinations).

first_principles.problem: One poison message in a Kinesis shard blocks processing for hours with endless retries.
truths: Polling is handled by Lambda, not your code.
Batch size trades latency for efficiency.
derivation: For streams: **bisect on error**, **max retry attempts**, **max record age**.
Use **event filtering** to skip irrelevant records.

analogy.title: A postal sorting crew that collects mail for you
analogy.story: They fetch bundles from the mailbox and hand them over; you tell them what to do with damaged letters.
analogy.breaks: Postal crews skip bad letters automatically; you must configure failure handling or streams stall.

check.a: Returning only failed record IDs so successful records in the batch aren't reprocessed.
